a: Death's ropes
t: Ropes, pangs or breakers of death?
p: The Psalm's Hebrew reads 'ropes' (or 'pangs'); the Samuel copy has 'breakers'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (Psalm 18:5 in Hebrew), as vowel-pointed
readings.plain: Death's ropes

readings.w: Septuagint, Psalm 17:5 (Rahlfs); Acts 2:24 uses the phrase
readings.plain: Death's birth pains

readings.w: 2 Samuel 22:5 (Masoretic Text)
readings.plain: Death's breakers

why: The consonants of the Psalm allow 'ropes' or 'pangs'; the next verse speaks of ropes and snares, so 'ropes' fits the picture best. Samuel's 'breakers' is a different word that matches the 'floods' of the next line; either could be original.

a: he swooped
p: Two letters that look almost the same in Hebrew give 'he swooped' in the Psalm and 'he was seen' in Samuel.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (Psalm 18:11 in Hebrew)
readings.plain: he swooped

readings.w: 2 Samuel 22:11 (Masoretic Text); some Hebrew manuscripts of the Psalm
readings.plain: he came into view

readings.w: Septuagint, Psalm 17:11 (Rahlfs)
readings.plain: he flew

why: Hebrew d (ד) and r (ר) are easily confused. 'Swooped', the verb for a bird of prey (Deuteronomy 28:49), fits the flying image of the line, and most scholars think Samuel's 'was seen' is the copying slip. The Greek repeats 'flew' for both verbs.

a: his voice, hail and fiery coals.
p: The words 'hail and fiery coals' close both 18:12 and 18:13. The Samuel copy and the Greek have them only once.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (Psalm 18:14 in Hebrew)
readings.en: gave his voice: hail and coals of fire
readings.plain: his voice, hail and fiery coals.

readings.w: 2 Samuel 22:14; Septuagint, Psalm 17:14 (Rahlfs); several Hebrew manuscripts
readings.plain: his voice.

why: The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew text of the Psalm, the base of this translation. Many scholars think the words were copied by mistake from the line above, since they spoil the balance of the verse and are missing from Samuel and the Greek; the shorter reading may well be original.

a: Yet their line has run out over the whole earth,
p: The Hebrew says 'their line'. The Greek says 'their sound', and Paul quotes the Greek in Romans 10:18.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (Psalm 19:5 in Hebrew); Targum
readings.plain: Yet their line has run out over the whole earth,

readings.w: Septuagint, Psalm 18:5 (Rahlfs); Jerome's Gallican Psalter (sonus); Romans 10:18; Syriac
readings.plain: Yet their sound has gone out over the whole earth,

why: The Hebrew 'their line' is the harder reading. A qav is a measuring cord (Jeremiah 31:39), so the sky's 'line' marks out the whole earth as its territory. The Greek 'sound' suits the talk of speech and words, and many scholars think the Greek read qolam, 'their voice', a very similar word. Paul, writing in Greek, quotes the Greek reading about the preaching of the gospel.
b: In Romans 10:18 Paul applies the line to the apostles' message reaching the world. He does not argue from the sky; he borrows the psalm's words.

a: from arrogant sins
p: The Hebrew zedim means 'arrogant' (people or acts). The Greek read 'strangers'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (Psalm 19:14 in Hebrew)
readings.plain: from arrogant sins

readings.w: Septuagint, Psalm 18:14 (Rahlfs); Jerome's Gallican Psalter (ab alienis)
readings.plain: from strangers

why: Zedim (from zed, 'arrogant') and zarim ('strangers') differ by one letter that looks much alike (ד and ר). The Hebrew fits the contrast with hidden faults in 19:12. Zedim usually means arrogant people (Psalm 119:21), so some translate 'keep your servant from the arrogant', but 'do not let them rule over me' fits sins that master a person (Genesis 4:7), and the Plain English Translation takes it so.

a: lift our flags
t: Raise banners, or be made great?
p: The Hebrew 'raise a banner' differs by one letter from 'be made great', which the Greek read.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (Psalm 20:6 in Hebrew)
readings.plain: lift our flags

readings.w: Septuagint, Psalm 19:6 (Rahlfs); Syriac
readings.plain: be made great

why: Nidgol ('raise a banner', from degel, a tribe's banner, Numbers 2:2) fits the scene of an army setting out. The Greek read the same letters in a different order, nigdal. The Hebrew is the harder and rarer word and is kept.

a: LORD, save!
t: Save the king, or 'May the King answer'?
p: The Hebrew accents divide the verse after 'save'. The Greek reads 'Lord, save the king, and answer us.'

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (Psalm 20:10 in Hebrew), by its accents
readings.en: LORD, save! The King, may he answer us
readings.plain: LORD, save!

readings.w: Septuagint, Psalm 19:10 (Rahlfs); Jerome's Gallican Psalter (Domine salvum fac regem)
readings.orig: κύριε σῶσον τὸν βασιλέα σου καὶ ἐπάκουσον ἡμῶν
readings.en: Lord, save the king, and hear us
readings.plain: LORD, save the king!

why: The accents of the Hebrew make 'the King' the subject of 'may he answer', so the King who answers is God, as in 24:10. The Greek joins 'the king' to 'save' and so prays for David's king. Both make sense; the Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew accents.
b: With the Greek reading, the second line would read 'and answer us on the day we call.' The Latin Domine, salvum fac regem was sung for the kings of France for centuries, and composers such as Charpentier set it to music.

a: My God, my God, why have you abandoned me?
p: The Greek adds 'listen to me' after 'my God'. The Gospels quote the cry without it.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (Psalm 22:2 in Hebrew); Mark 15:34; Matthew 27:46
readings.en: My God, my God, why have you abandoned me?
readings.plain: My God, my God, why have you abandoned me?

readings.w: Septuagint, Psalm 21:2 (Rahlfs); Jerome's Gallican Psalter (respice me)
readings.orig: ὁ θεὸς ὁ θεός μου πρόσχες μοι ἵνα τί ἐγκατέλιπές με
readings.en: God, my God, attend to me; why have you forsaken me?
readings.plain: God, my God, listen to me; why have you abandoned me?

why: The Hebrew is shorter, and Mark and Matthew quote it in that form. The Greek words 'attend to me' are probably an addition, perhaps from 22:19 ('hurry to my help').

a: from the words I roar out.
p: The Greek read 'the words of my transgressions', a word that looks like 'my roaring'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex
readings.plain: from the words I roar out.

readings.w: Septuagint, Psalm 21:2 (Rahlfs); Jerome's Gallican Psalter (verba delictorum meorum)
readings.plain: from the words of my sins.

why: Sha'agati ('my roaring') and shegagati ('my error') differ by one letter. The Hebrew fits the cry and the lions of the psalm. The Greek gave the church a problem: how could Christ speak of 'my sins'? Augustine answered that Christ speaks here for his body, the church.

a: Roll it onto the LORD! Let the LORD get him free!
p: The Hebrew vowels make 'roll' a command; the Greek, the Syriac and Matthew 27:43 read a past tense, 'he hoped' or 'he trusted'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (gol, imperative)
readings.plain: Roll it onto the LORD! Let the LORD get him free!

readings.w: Septuagint, Psalm 21:9 (Rahlfs: ēlpisen epi kyrion, checked); Syriac; compare Matthew 27:43 (consonants read as gal, 'he rolled')
readings.plain: He hoped in the LORD; let the LORD get him free!

why: The consonants can be read either way. The Masoretic vowels give a command, the mockers' sarcastic advice to a man who says he trusts God, and that fits the jeering of 22:7. The Greek read the same letters as a statement about his past trust, and Matthew 27:43 echoes that form. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew and supplies 'it'.

a: Like a lion, they go for my hands and feet.
t: Like a lion, or they pierced?
p: The most debated reading in the Psalms. The Hebrew has 'like a lion'; the oldest Greek and a Dead Sea copy seem to have a verb.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (Psalm 22:17 in Hebrew), and nearly all medieval Hebrew manuscripts; Targum ('biting like a lion')
readings.en: like a lion, my hands and my feet
readings.plain: Like a lion, they go for my hands and feet.

readings.w: Septuagint, Psalm 21:17 (Rahlfs: ōryxan, 'they dug'); Syriac Peshitta ('they pierced'); Jerome's Gallican Psalter (foderunt); 5/6HevPs from Nahal Hever, first century AD (k'rw, a verb form, as read by Flint); a few medieval Hebrew manuscripts (k'rw)
readings.en: they dug (bored through) my hands and my feet
readings.plain: They have pierced my hands and my feet.

readings.w: Aquila's second edition and Symmachus (second century AD), Greek; Jerome's Psalter iuxta Hebraeos (vinxerunt, as usually printed)
readings.en: they bound my hands and my feet
readings.plain: They have bound my hands and my feet.

readings.w: Modern conjecture from a root meaning 'shrink, shrivel' (so the NRSV)
readings.en: my hands and feet are shriveled
readings.plain: My hands and feet have shriveled.

why: The Plain English Translation follows the Leningrad Codex, the base text of this translation, which reads ka'ari, 'like a lion'. It fits the lion of 22:13 and 22:21, and the Targum read it so. But the reading is far from certain: the Hebrew line has no verb, the Greek (about 200 BC, long before Christian debates) and the first-century Nahal Hever scroll seem to have a verb, and most Christian translations follow 'pierced'. To make an English sentence, the Plain English Translation supplies 'they go for', which the Hebrew does not have. The reader can switch readings here.
b:
The difference in Hebrew is one stroke: k'ry (with yod, 'like a lion') against k'rw (with waw, a verb 'they dug'). In the Nahal Hever copy (5/6HevPs, published by Peter Flint in DJD 38) the last letter is a waw. Some scholars caution that yod and waw are often hard to tell apart in hands of this period; Flint reads waw. The verb karah means 'dig' (as a well or pit), and its normal spelling has no aleph; 'dig into hands' is an odd phrase, which is why some prefer 'bind' (Vall) or 'shrivel'. Strawn defends 'like a lion' on the strength of the psalm's imagery. Aquila's first edition is reported as 'they disfigured'.

Which reading a translation follows has long carried the weight of the Jewish-Christian argument (see the note on 'Like a lion'). A fair summary is that the Christian reading did not invent a verb, since one stands in old Greek and Hebrew witnesses, and that the Jewish reading did not invent a lion, since it stands in the main Hebrew tradition.

a: From the horns of the wild oxen you have answered me.
p: The Hebrew ends with 'you have answered me'. The Greek read 'my lowliness', so the plea continues.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (Psalm 22:22 in Hebrew)
readings.en: and from the horns of wild oxen you have answered me
readings.plain: From the horns of the wild oxen you have answered me.

readings.w: Septuagint, Psalm 21:22 (Rahlfs); Jerome's Gallican Psalter (humilitatem meam)
readings.orig: καὶ ἀπὸ κεράτων μονοκερώτων τὴν ταπείνωσίν μου
readings.en: and from the horns of unicorns my lowliness
readings.plain: and save my lowly life from the horns of the wild oxen.

why: The Greek read 'aniyyati, 'my affliction', for 'anitani, 'you answered me'. The Hebrew is abrupt, and many modern translations change it, but its abruptness is the point: the answer breaks in, and the rest of the psalm is thanks.

a: the one who could not keep himself alive.
t: 'He could not keep himself alive', or 'I will live for him'?
p: The Hebrew is obscure. The Greek reads 'and my soul lives for him'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (Psalm 22:30 in Hebrew)
readings.en: and his soul he did not keep alive
readings.plain: the one who could not keep himself alive.

readings.w: Septuagint, Psalm 21:30 (Rahlfs); Syriac; Jerome's Gallican Psalter (anima mea illi vivet)
readings.orig: καὶ ἡ ψυχή μου αὐτῷ ζῇ
readings.en: and my soul lives for him
readings.plain: and I will live for him.

why: The Hebrew has 'his soul' (nafsho) and 'not' (lo'); the Greek read 'my soul' (nafshi) and 'for him' (lo, sounded the same). The Hebrew is harder but makes sense: even the dying, who cannot keep themselves alive, will kneel. Many modern translations follow the Greek and join it to the next verse.

a: A line of descendants will serve him;
p: The Greek has 'my seed will serve him'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex
readings.plain: A line of descendants will serve him;

readings.w: Septuagint, Psalm 21:31 (Rahlfs); Jerome's Gallican Psalter (semen meum)
readings.orig: καὶ τὸ σπέρμα μου δουλεύσει αὐτῷ
readings.en: and my seed will serve him
readings.plain: My descendants will serve him;

why: The Greek's 'my' goes with its 'my soul' in the verse before. The Hebrew 'seed' is general: the generations to come.

a: and I will come back to the house of the LORD
p: As pointed, the Hebrew says 'I will return'. The Greek, Syriac and most translations have 'I will live'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex, as vowel-pointed
readings.plain: and I will come back to the house of the LORD

readings.w: Septuagint, Psalm 22:6 (Rahlfs: to katoikein me, 'my dwelling'); Syriac; Jerome (ut inhabitem); Symmachus
readings.plain: and I will live in the house of the LORD

why: The vowels of the Hebrew give shavti, 'I will return', from shuv. The consonants could also be a shortened form of yashavti, 'I will dwell', which the Greek and the other ancient versions read and which fits 'in the house of the LORD'. Both make good sense: a pilgrim's hope to come back to the temple again and again, or a hope to stay there. The Plain English Translation keeps the pointed Hebrew.

a: who has not lifted up his soul to what is empty
p: The Leningrad Codex writes 'my soul'; the margin of Masoretic Bibles, many Hebrew manuscripts and the Greek have 'his soul'.

readings.w: Many Hebrew manuscripts and the Masoretic margin (Qere); Septuagint, Psalm 23:4 (Rahlfs: tēn psychēn autou); Jerome's Gallican Psalter (animam suam)
readings.plain: who has not lifted up his soul to what is empty

readings.w: Leningrad Codex, as written
readings.plain: who has not lifted up my soul to what is empty

why: Grammar wants 'his soul', and most witnesses have it, so the Plain English Translation follows them. The Leningrad reading 'my soul' makes God the speaker: the person 'who has not lifted up my soul (that is, my self, my name) to emptiness', a close echo of Exodus 20:7. Some scholars think that is the original and that 'his' smoothed it out.

a: who search for your face, O Jacob.
t: 'Your face, Jacob', or 'the face of the God of Jacob'?
p: The Hebrew reads 'your face, Jacob'. The Greek and Syriac have 'the face of the God of Jacob'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex; Targum
readings.plain: who search for your face, O Jacob.

readings.w: Septuagint, Psalm 23:6 (Rahlfs); Syriac
readings.orig: ζητούντων τὸ πρόσωπον τοῦ θεοῦ Ιακωβ
readings.en: seeking the face of the God of Jacob
readings.plain: who search for the face of the God of Jacob.

why: The Hebrew is hard: God is not elsewhere called 'Jacob', and people do not seek Jacob's face. 'Jacob' may be addressed ('O Jacob', as the King James Version has it), or it may stand beside the seekers ('they are Jacob'), saying that they are the true Israel; the new Jewish Publication Society version has 'Jacob, who seek Your presence'. The Greek smooths this by adding 'God of'. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew and takes Jacob as addressed.

a: This is the company of those who seek him,
p: The written Hebrew has 'one who seeks him'; the margin and most witnesses have the plural.

readings.w: Masoretic margin (Qere); Leningrad Codex as pointed; Septuagint
readings.plain: This is the company of those who seek him,

readings.w: Masoretic consonants (Ketiv)
readings.plain: This is the company of the one who seeks him,

why: The difference is one letter and does not change the sense much. The plural fits 'company' and the plural 'who search' that follows.

a: If I had not trusted that I would see the LORD's goodness
p: The Hebrew starts with 'if not', marked with dots by the scribes as doubtful. The Greek leaves it out.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (with extraordinary dots over lule')
readings.en: if I had not believed that I would see
readings.plain: If I had not trusted that I would see the LORD's goodness

readings.w: Septuagint, Psalm 26:13 (Rahlfs: pisteuō tou idein); Jerome's Gallican Psalter (credo videre); Syriac
readings.en: I believe that I will see
readings.plain: I trust that I will see the LORD's goodness

why: The scribes who copied the Hebrew put dots above and below lule', 'if not', a sign that they doubted the word. Without it the line is a plain statement of faith, as in the Greek. With it the sentence breaks off: 'If I had not believed ...' (what then?). The Plain English Translation keeps the word, as the Leningrad Codex does, and shows the break with dots; the reader can switch.
b: The Masoretes marked fifteen places in the Hebrew Bible with these 'extraordinary points' (Hebrew nequdot); 27:13 is the only one in the Psalms. Rabbinic tradition explained the dots as David's doubt whether he would share in the world to come (Bavli Berakhot 4a).

a: and I will thank him out of my song.
p: The Greek read the last lines as 'my flesh has flourished again, and willingly I will thank him'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex
readings.en: and from my song I will thank him
readings.plain: and I will thank him out of my song.

readings.w: Septuagint, Psalm 27:7 (Rahlfs: kai anethalen hē sarx mou kai ek thelēmatos mou exomologēsomai autō)
readings.orig: καὶ ἀνέθαλεν ἡ σάρξ μου καὶ ἐκ θελήματός μου
readings.en: and my flesh revived, and from my will I will thank him
readings.plain: and my body grew strong again, and gladly I will thank him.

why: The Greek seems to have read a different Hebrew in the line before ('my flesh' for 'my heart') and read mishiri, 'from my song', as 'from my will'. The Hebrew is clear and natural: the rescued person thanks God with a song.

a: The LORD is strength for them;
p: The Hebrew says 'for them'; some Hebrew manuscripts, the Greek and the Syriac say 'for his people'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex
readings.en: the LORD is strength for them
readings.plain: The LORD is strength for them;

readings.w: Some Hebrew manuscripts; Septuagint, Psalm 27:8 (Rahlfs: kyrios krataiōma tou laou autou); Syriac
readings.en: the LORD is strength for his people
readings.plain: The LORD is strength for his people;

why: Lamo ('for them') and le'ammo ('for his people') differ by one letter. 'His people' fits the parallel with 'his anointed' and the closing prayer for 'your people' (28:9), and many translations follow it. The Hebrew 'them' can refer to God's people too, and is kept.

a: you sons of the gods,
t: A double line in the Greek
p: The Greek has 'Bring to the Lord, you sons of God, bring to the Lord young rams'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex
readings.plain: you sons of the gods,

readings.w: Septuagint, Psalm 28:1 (Rahlfs); Jerome's Gallican Psalter (afferte Domino filios arietum)
readings.orig: υἱοὶ θεοῦ ἐνέγκατε τῷ κυρίῳ υἱοὺς κριῶν
readings.en: sons of God; bring to the Lord young rams
readings.plain: you sons of God; give to the LORD young rams,

why: The Greek translated benei 'elim twice: once as 'sons of God' and once as 'sons of rams' ('ayil, 'ram'). The second is a double translation, not a second Hebrew line.

a: so I did not go down into the pit.
t: 'From going down', or 'from among those who go down'?
p: The written Hebrew has 'from those who go down to the pit'; the spoken text has 'from my going down'.

readings.w: Masoretic margin (Qere), as the Leningrad Codex is pointed; many Hebrew manuscripts
readings.en: from my going down to the pit
readings.plain: so I did not go down into the pit.

readings.w: Masoretic consonants (Ketiv); Septuagint, Psalm 29:4 (Rahlfs: apo tōn katabainontōn eis lakkon); Jerome
readings.en: from among those who go down to the pit
readings.plain: from among those who go down into the pit.

why: Both readings mean that God saved him from death. The spoken text (Qere) makes it his own descent; the written text and the Greek make him one of the dying whom God pulled back. The Plain English Translation follows the vowels of the Leningrad Codex.

a: so that glory may make music to you
p: The Hebrew has 'glory' alone; the Greek has 'my glory', and many scholars read 'my glory' or 'my liver' (the inmost self).

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex
readings.plain: so that glory may make music to you

readings.w: Septuagint, Psalm 29:13 (Rahlfs: hē doxa mou, checked); Syriac
readings.plain: so that my glory may make music to you

readings.w: Conjecture (kevedi, 'my liver', or kevodi, 'my glory')
readings.plain: so that my inmost self may make music to you

why: The Hebrew makes sense as it stands: 'glory' can mean the self (as in 16:9 and 57:8, where it has 'my'). The Greek's 'my' may be a translator's help or may reflect a Hebrew copy with one more letter. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew. The Greek also ends the line 'and I will not be stung (with grief)' where the Hebrew has 'and not go quiet'.
